Tomahawk, mani̍htsip-ihpse (an French; e distinctly pronounced).
Woman (wife), mi̍a (mi run together; a separated; the whole short).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [243] Written from the pronunciation of a Crow Indian. They pronounce the words in the manner of the Minnitarri; ch is guttural, r is spoken with the point of the tongue unless there is an exception noted. According to Donald Mc Kenzie who lived among the Crows (Gallatin, ibid., p. 125), they number some three hundred lodges and three thousand souls. This seems to me to be a correct estimate.—Maximilian.
Comment by Ed. Gallatin doubtless intends Kenneth (not Donald) Mc Kenzie, for whom see our volume xxi, p. 45, note 25.
[244] According to Captain Bonneville, it is called popo in the Crow language; this does not agree with my experience.—Maximilian.
Comment by Ed. This refers to Washington Irving, Rocky Mountains; or Scenes, Incidents and Adventures in the Far West (Philadelphia, 1837).

div.head: DACOTA (Sioux) of the band of the Yanktonans[245]
div.p: American, Mi̍na-haska (haska nasal); i.e., Long Knife.
Blind, ischtá-chon-gä (ch guttural; on French; g in the roof of the mouth; chonga nasal and without emphasis).
Bow, itáh-sipa (itah with emphasis; si very short; pa without emphasis).
Brave (adj), uadi̍take (uadi with emphasis; e ½ or a little more; take lower and without emphasis).
Brother, tschi̍-ä (emphasis on the first syllable).
Door, thiópa (i and o somewhat separated).
Dream (v), uihamana (ui together; hamana short and rapid).
Ear, nónchä (on French; emphasis on non; ch guttural; low and short).
Englishman, Sakedaschi (e short; i barely audible).
Evening, chta-ié-tu (chta guttural; ie together; tu short).
Feather, uï̍-iak-ha (ha guttural; iakha low and short).
Frenchman, Uaschi̍djo (jo French and very short).
God (the creator), uakán-tanka (an French nasal); i.e., great spirit.[246]
Good, uaschtä̍ (ua almost like wa; run together).
Gun, mansak-han (an French; the whole run together).
Healthy, uaschtä̍; or uaiá-saschni (last word short and low); i.e., not sick.
Horns (antlers; and horns of all animals in general), hä; the name of the animal is added.
Hunger, wóta-wacheda (all syllables of second word even).
Hunt (v), uïheni (e short; the whole indistinct, short, nasal, and run together).
Ice, tschága (g in the roof of the mouth).
Island, uï̍hta (u and i separated; ta short).
Morning, hi̍h-hanna (emphasis on hih; hanna low and short).
Pipe (tobacco), schandúh-hupa (hupa short and low, without emphasis).
Revenge (v), itoh-kidjuh (emphasis on first word; j French; second word lower).
River, uathpá; the Missouri, Uathpá-mnischoschá; i.e., the river with muddy water.
Spirits (distilled), meni̍h-uakán (an French); i.e. divine, or medicine water.
Stingy, ocha̍n-schitscha (ochan with emphasis; second word without emphasis; the whole short and run together).
Sweet, skúia (sk with the point of the tongue).
Thunder, uaki̍n-a (n French, nasal; a short).
Tomahawk, onspä̍-tschanupa (final word without emphasis and lower).
Trader, wópäton-uïtschásta (o full; on French; last word short).
Village, otón-a (on French; a short; the whole nasal).
Wash (v), waiújaja (jaja French, without emphasis, and low; iu German).
Winter, uani̍ete (u and a separated; e very short in both cases).
Five, sáhptan (s very soft; an French).
Nine, nahptschi̍-uanká (uan nasal; n French; last word without emphasis, nasal, and low; the whole run together and short).
Ten, uïktschémna (u and i separated; na short).
Twenty-one, uïktschemna-nom-sommuaji (the whole run together and short; ji French).
Hundred, opánuachä (an French; u and a separated; ch guttural; the whole run together and short; uacha nasal).
Thousand, iktó-panuachä (an French; the whole run together and short).
I eat, uauáhta (u and a separated).
He eats, uóhtä (u and o like w; o full; ta short).
We eat, o̍ntape (in pronouncing tape the voice falls; pe distinctly pronounced).
I shall eat, uauáhtäkta (u and a separated; takta low and without emphasis).
I would eat, hähan-uauáhta-net-schetscha (last word short and rapid).
Antelope, tatóhka; or tatókana (na rather inaudible).
Bear, (black), uachánk-sitscha (emphasis on chank; sitscha low).
Buffalo (bull), tatánka; cow, ptäh; calf, ptäh-sidja (j French); the general word is that for cow.
Elk, upán (pan nasal; an French); this is the general word.
Horse, schónka-uakán (on and an French): erratum says read i̍hia.
Skunk, mankáh (an French, very short, and barely audible; kah loud and with emphasis).
Turkey (wild), sisitscha-kanka (s soft; kan in the throat).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [245] Gallatin writes "Dahcota;" but I think that it is more correct to write Dacóta. He divides the Sioux into a northern and a southern group; and includes in the latter division eight tribes, the Quappas, or Arkansas at the mouth of the Arkansa river, the Osages, the Kansas, the Ayowäs (Jowas), the Missouris, Otos, Omáhas, and Puncas, since they speak dialects of the Dacóta language (Gallatin, ibid., p. 127).—Maximilian.

[246] Not wakatunka, as Vail says. This name is composed of two words; and, therefore, is not to be written as one. The first word, uakan, less correctly wakan, is the expression for god, divine, supernatural; the second, tanka, not tunka, means great. Vail and others also very often write uakan, incorrectly wah-kon. The Dacóta words which I give here are written from the pronunciation of the half-breed interpreter, Ortubize.—Maximilian.
Comment by Ed. This reference is to Eugene A. Vail, Notice sur les Indiens de l'Amerique du Nord (Paris, 1840).

[247] Mr. Gallatin (ibid., p. 195) thinks that the word uitschá is an abbreviation of uitschasta. I cannot decide the question with certainty. The singular number, man, was always given to me as uitscha; uitschasta seems to me to be the plural, or a general term, as for instance, in the word uitschasta-iuta, man eater.—Maximilian.

div.head: DACOTA of the Teton Tribe
div.p: Bear (black), wåchánk-sitscha (the first word with emphasis).
Day (the day breaks), àm-pa-inam-pä (am French; pa short).
Elk, upán (an French and rather long); the stag, hächáhka.
Shield, oahát-sanka (first word with emphasis; last word low and without emphasis).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [248] The variations in the different tribes of the Dacótas seem to be very insignificant.—Maximilian.

div.head: FALL INDIANS, or Grosventres of the Prairies[249]
div.p: Arrow, nennitch (ch with the point of the tongue and not guttural).
Bear (grizzly), uosse (uo like wo; e very short).
Beaver, hábass (a almost like a umlaut, but ½ and short).
Black, wå-atåh-nits (wa short; atah-nits a little lisped).
Buffalo (bull), enáhkiä (e barely audible; kia like kie, short and ½).
Child, tä̍yalle (all syllables cut rather short and separated; e ½).
Day, e̍hse (eh long; se very short).
Ear, nenottónnü (ton with emphasis; e ½).
Earth, meth-auuch (au together; auuch very short).
Eye, ne-séh-seh (ne short and ½; accent on the first seh).
Foot, nesse-estan (se short and ½; tan French and distinct).
God, mehåa (e short; the two a's separated).
Hot, be-ke-néh-se (be rather longer; ke short; neh very long; se short).
Leg, na-áhtz (na short and ½; ahtz long).
Night, taiké-ee (ee separated and distinctly pronounced).
Snow, i̍h-i (ih very long; i short).
Star, a̍to (o almost like o umlaut).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [249] Written from their pronunciation. They call their tribe, Ä̍hni-ninn. Gallatin (ibid., p. 125) speaks of them in connection with the Minnitarris. He calls them the Rapid, Fall, or Paunch Indians; and remarks quite correctly, that from the latest information their language is wholly different from those of the Minnitarris and Blackfeet (ibid., p. 132).—Maximilian.

div.head: FLATHEADS of the Rocky Mountains[250]
div.p: Bow, soh-nónn; same word as for gun.
Buffalo, zotúnn (soft low, and indistinct; o full).
Child, skochkússa (ch guttural; sa low and indistinct).
Deer, zinechkóhch (ch guttural; the whole indistinct and low).
Elk, chton-skutsiss (ch guttural; the whole indistinct and low).
Fire, stehchke (st with the point of the tongue; ch guttural; final e ½).
God, inuméhcho (i like e; ch guttural).
Moon, ehs-pach-kann (low and in the roof of the mouth).
Mouth, onuchuaye (ch guttural; final e ½).
Pipe (tobacco), simä̍h-noch (simah short; noch guttural; little emphasis).
Star, skoch-koiomm (low and run together; och guttural).
Sun, ehs-pach-kann (low and in the roof of the mouth).
Woman, semääm (e ½; a and a separated).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [250] Written from the pronunciation of the Blackfoot chief, Ninoch-Kiä̍iu. The Flatheads live in the Rocky mountains; and according to the missionary, Parker, number only eight hundred souls. They are said to speak the same language as the Ponderas [Pend d'Oreille] and Spokein [Spokan] Indians. The custom of flattening the head by pressure is not found among them, at least at present (Townsend, op. cit., p. 175); but this is done by several tribes on the Columbia as is stated also in Astoria. All travellers who have visited this people bear witness to their upright and noble conduct, as well as to their piety. Like the Nez-Percés, of whom the same is said, they have borrowed a number of Christian usages and beliefs, among them the conscientious observance of Sunday (see Adventures of Captain Bonneville, p. 248; and Ross Cox). They are reputed to be brave warriors; of this I was assured by the Blackfoot Indians themselves, who are often at war with them and are their bitterest enemies, and who also showed me many trophies taken from them.—Maximilian.

Comment by Ed. Samuel Parker, Journal of an Exploring Tour beyond the Rocky Mountains (Ithaca, N. Y., 1838). See also our volume xxi, p. 335, note 112; Washington Irving, Astoria (Philadelphia, 1836); Ross Cox, Adventures upon the Columbia River (London, 1831); and our volume vi, p. 276, note 84.

div.head: KICKAPU[251]
div.p: Bow, måstahá (a between a umlaut and o umlaut; ha often barely audible).
Hand, nenä̍chkonn (ach in the roof of the mouth).
Leg, nemóttata (a somewhat as if with umlaut).
Water, neppé (final e somewhat like a umlaut).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [251] Written from the pronunciation of a Ki̍ckapu. These Indians speak the same language as the Saukis and Foxes. According to Gallatin (ibid., p. 62), they do not now number over five hundred souls. They all live at present west of the Mississippi.—Maximilian.

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [252] The Konsas, or Kansas Indians have always lived on the river of that name (Gallatin, ibid., p. 127). For the past thirty years they have lived at peace with the Osages; and the two tribes have intermarried. They still number fifteen hundred souls, and possess a tract of three thousand acres. They speak the Osage dialect, which belongs to the Dacota linguistic group.—Maximilian.

div.head: KRIH, or Knistenau[253]
div.p: American (an), Ketsemohkoman (e short and ½; otherwise German).
Bird, piesiss (i and e separated; e full value).
Brave (adj), sohketäheu (e ½; eu short; u barely audible).
Cold (adj), kesinnau (e ½; au German and together).
Dance (v), neméhetu (second e ½; tu short).
Deaf, kakehpi-teu (pi like pich, guttural; e and u separated).
Devil (evil spirit), matsimann-tuh (short and run together).
Dumb, namanich-tauéu (manich short and guttural; e and u separated).
Ear, ochtauakay (ch guttural; aua separated; kay German, with the rest of the word).
Father, nochtauï (noch nasal; ch German, but barely audible).
Feather, meh-koánn (koann very short and run together).
Flesh, wuiïäs (wui almost like wi or ui).
Heat, ksasteo (eo short and half pronounced).
House (lodge), uaskaëgan; i.e., house of the white man; matsehkin, a leather tent.
Hunger, notä̍-keteu (keteu short; u barely audible).
I, neia̍ (emphasis on ia, which is very short).
Lightning, uauase-skutä̍-paiú (e ½; emphasis on second word; last word lower).
Negro, keskiteuias (e short and ½; e and u separated).
Quick, kiépa (e ½; pa short; i and e separated).
Red (the color), mechkossúh (ch barely audible and with the point of the tongue).
Small, apsáhsinn (sin very short and without emphasis).
Spring (the season), meiuskamin (short; n French; in almost like i nasal).
Thunder, piéh-su (pronounced together; su without emphasis).
War, notintuock (u and o separated and barely audible).
Woman (wife), iskwä̍u (au separated; u barely audible).
They reckon the months from one full moon to the next. [The order here given is that of the original.—Ed.]
November, Kaskattinoh-pisimm; i.e., the ice moon.
January, Kesäh-pisimm (e ½); i.e., the big moon.
February, Paua-zakenassis-pisimm (a and u separated; za short and like a); i.e., the moon which shakes the trees.
March, Mekssiuh-pisimm (e short and ½; siuh almost like suh); i.e., the moon when the eagle comes.
----, Niski-pisimm; i.e., the moon of the wild geese.
----, Ayiki-pisimm; i.e., the moon of the frogs.
May, Opineya-uäu-pisimm (uau separated), i.e., moon when the birds lay their eggs.
June, Opaskoh-pisimm; i.e., the moon when the geese shed their feathers.
July, Oochpahoh-pisimm (ooch guttural); i.e., moon when the birds fly.
----, Onont-chicheto (on French; tch with the point of the tongue; e ½); i.e., moon when the buffalo is in heat.
October, Opinna-skoh-pisimm; i.e., the moon when the leaves fall.
Five, neanann (e full value and separated from a).
Eight, aehnaneu (a and e separated; ne and u separated and short).
Thousand, kich-tche-mta-tach-tommetano (ich, tch, and ch with the point of the tongue; e ½).
Antelope, apestat-jéhkus (e ½; j French; jeh with emphasis; kus low and without emphasis).
Elk, uauasskéhsu (su short and barely audible).
Sit down and smoke and relate to us, a-péh-pit-tuá-ah-tsimo.
Whence do you come? tan-täh-kotuch-tann (ch guttural).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [253] Written from the pronunciation of a Krih Indian.—Maximilian.

div.head: KUTANÄ, or Kutnehä̍[254]
div.p: Arrow, a̍hk (k prolonged as a guttural).
Black, kamokoch-kukossni (ch guttural; the whole very short and indistinct).
Blue, confused by most tribes with green and given the same name.
Bow, zü̍pil (i very short, indistinct, and almost like e).
Foot, achksikkis (ch guttural; k clicked with the tongue; final i like e).
Hair, akuksammus (k lisped with the tongue).
Man, aks-macki (a slight pause after aks).
Moon, same word as for sun.
Night, zesmuiet (indistinct; iet like et, distinctly pronounced but short).
Pipe (tobacco), achkússa (ch and the whole guttural and low).
Rain, esuch-kukuttunn (very short and indistinct; guttural).
Red, kanóhs (a almost like e; short and low).
Snow, achksoh (ks like sch with a clicking of the tongue).
Star, akisnohs (s with a peculiar clicking sound).
Sun, natánnik (k barely audible, only a slight guttural sound).
Tomahawk, achkensä (ks with a clicking of the tongue, like sch).
White, kamonuckso (so with a clicking of the tongue).
Yellow, kemacktze (first e ½; final e distinctly pronounced).
Bear (grizzly), ksaus (German; s with a clicking of the tongue, like sch).
Deer, zupka (u between u and o).
Dog, cháhtsin (ch guttural; a almost as if with umlaut).
Elk, keskásse (sk with a clicking of the tongue).
Mountain goat (white), zenúchcho (ch guttural; the whole run together).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [254] Written from the pronunciation of the old Kutanä̍ Indian, Hómach-Ksáchkum, the Great Earth, of whom a most excellent likeness is given on Plate 79 of my Atlas. I have spoken of this people in several places in the first volume of this work. Parker (ibid., p. 304) says of the Kutonä̍s, Kutnehä̍s, or Kutanihs: "The Cootanies inhabit a section of country to the north of the Ponderas along M'Gillivray's river, and they are represented as an uncommonly interesting people. They speak a language distinct from all the tribes about them, open and sonorous, and free from gutturals, which are common in the language of the surrounding tribes. They are neat in their persons and lodges, candid and honest, and kind to each other. I could not ascertain their numbers, but probably they are not over a thousand." In Ross Cox, (p. 242), there is also information regarding them; but the missionary Parker (ibid., p. 286) seems to call this traveller's truthfulness in question. From my carefully copied words of the Kutanä language, it is evident that it is not easy to pronounce on account of its lingual clicking; and that it has a large number of guttural tones.—Maximilian.

[255] The Kutanä̍s, or Kutunä̍s, also Kutnehä̍s, dwell in the Rocky mountains beyond the sources of Maria river; and on their mountains lives the white mountain goat. They are said to call themselves Kutonachä; the French know them as Coutonais; and the Blackfeet call them Kutanä̍. They are few in number, having only some forty lodges. Among their ornaments they highly prize cylinders cut from mussel-shells, especially those cut from the shell of the dentalium, which they obtain from the western seacoast. The Blackfeet, especially the Blood Indians, are their declared enemies. They do not live on the flesh of the buffalo, which is not found in their mountains; but in their country many beaver are obtained, excellent fish (trout), and several other species of animals, especially the orignal (cervus alces amer.), the white mountain goat, and the bighorn; also many kinds of roots and berries serve them as food. They raise large numbers of strong and handsome horses; they are well clothed; and are expert beaver hunters. They are skilful in making bows and arrows. Their language is difficult to learn. The words are spoken softly and indistinctly; in addition there are many clicking tones and hollow gutturals; and they also lisp.—Maximilian.

div.head: MANDAN, or Númangkake[256]
div.p: All (everything), ekúnhä (n French, like oun); all men, or people, a̍mbä (m French).
Always, amánkahu-sch (an French; husch run together as a final syllable).
American (n), Mánhichtä (an French; ch guttural); i.e., Long Knife.
Another, táhonsch (on French; honsch lower and shorter than ta).
Approach stealthily (v), cherúhradéhusch (che guttural; r with the point of the tongue).
Back (n), (v; to move with a jerk?), nápp-chä (ch guttural).
Back (adv), kiri̍je (je French); i.e., he is back, (il est deretour).
Bald, pah-e-sérroko-sch (e ½ and barely audible).
Ball (for playing), mihp-toht-kisch (pronounce together); the game is called by the same name.
Ball (same word as for lead), uáhtöschemáhhä (o almost like e; e only ½).
Ball-game of the women, mi̍hptott-kä̍; ball, mi̍hptodä̍.
Basket (leather; used by women for carrying), chä̍hank (ch guttural).
Belly, ä̍hchi (ah long and accented; ch guttural).
Below (beneath), mánpeta (an French; e ½; ta short).
Big with young, same word as for pregnant.
Bile (the yellow water on the stomach), wáh-sih-dä (da low and short).
Bill (bill or beak of a bird), same word as for nose.
Bite (v), naschä-sch (run together; ch slightly hissed).
Blind (adj), istá-chädetosch (ch guttural; chade short; the whole run together).
Blond, pahi̍n-si̍hdusch (n French; hin like hi nasal).
Bloom (v), hóh-säddähosch (hoh accented; second word short; sch sometimes slightly hissed).
Blush (v), stassä̍härreh (st with the point of the tongue).
Bough, does not occur in the singular; boughs, o̍hchancha (ch guttural).
Bow, woraërúhpa (e full, distinct, and short), or waraërúhpa; this is the bow of elm.
Bow (strengthened with elk or sheep horn), wahú-erúhpa.
Box on the ear, rotkä̍sch (r with the point of the tongue).
Breast, táchärächä (ch guttural; r with the point of the tongue).
Bridge (tree-bridge), mánna-achkini̍hnde (second word without emphasis; ach guttural).
Broom, i̍ngka-gischka (ing German; second word low).
Brown, tkópp: that is brown, anttkopposch (an French); it is brown, tkópposch.
Burn (v), ratsiposch: the prairie burns, máh-ódisch; i.e., the prairie is colored black.
Burn (v, tr or intr; destroy by fire), náchuhdusch (ch guttural).
Canoe (of leather), minnánke (an French; ke short and low).
Collar, warapening-gä (e ½; the whole run together).
Comb, pai̍wachunkä (ch guttural; ai together; ka short).
Come here (imperative), hú-ta (first syllable long; last syllable very short).
Console (v), kehápp-herrisch (e distinctly pronounced; herrisch short; the whole run together).
Corpse, uattä̍h-hädde (e distinctly pronounced; the whole run together).
Cowardly, wakarrachkáhsch (rr with the point of the tongue; ach guttural).
Crack (v; crack a whip), karaparaschusch (r full, with the point of the tongue).
Crow (way of wearing the hair), pahi̍n-okaskäsch (sch slightly hissed).
Cut (v), pauä̍-schusch (run together; paua short; a and u separated).
Cut down (a tree), mánna-kassähherrisch (herrisch very short and run together; the last two words pronounced together).
Dark, hapä̍hreschka (pah long; ka half short).
Day after to-morrow, mahtke-óhmaestá (e barely articulated, heard only as a light sound).
Deaf, nakóckä-sidikosch (ch guttural; the whole run together).
Deceive (they say "he has not paid his debts"), i̍hscha-häuahma-kuï-néhchusch (ch guttural; e distinctly pronounced).
Decoy (v; an animal), wattáchakhuhrosch (ch guttural); i.e., because I imitate their call, I make them come.
Delay (v; make late), o̍hhi-kahunuahärrisch (hun run together, like French oun; the whole short and pronounced together).
Demolish (v; e.g., take down a lodge), ohséhrusch (rusch low).
Devil (evil spirit), o̍mahank-chikä̍ (an French; ch guttural).
Dew, béddädä (e distinctly pronounced; the whole short).
Dirty, warát-keddisch (run together; keddisch short; e full value).
Do (v), isä̍kosch; do not do it, káhdä-isä̍ckta.
Draw (v; draw water), i̍nnisusch (run together; short).
Dream (n), same word as for verb.
Drum (n), mánna-berächä̍ (e distinctly pronounced; ch guttural).
Dust, uaratä̍; it is dusty, uaratä̍dachingkosch.
Ear-ornament, uóhkaske (e distinctly pronounced and short).
Earth, máhhankä (an French; ka short and low).
Elbow, akschi̍sche-náhde (first e ½; final e distinctly pronounced).
Englishman, Uaschi̍, or Waschi̍mihsiháhkta; i.e., a Frenchman from the north.
Even (flat), kahósta; really a level prairie or plain.
Everywhere, äkunhä-ahkskä-üahä̍rrisch (the two last words short and run together).
Eyelid, istá-rupchä (ch guttural; the whole run together).
Fail (v; miss), kakáhon-sch (kakahonsch; on French; honsch short and low).
Fall (v; of the leaves), haráhrusch (r with the point of the tongue): mánna-ahpöharáhrusch, the leaves are falling; mánna-ahpó, the leaves.
---- (your), ráhtosch (r with the point of the tongue); the plural is never used, they say instead "the father."
Finger, ungkáh-hä (ha very short and lower).
Fire, uáradä (ua nearly like wa; da distinctly pronounced and short).
Fish (v; catch fish), póhru-pschikóhsch (first e with the point of the tongue).
Flee (v; escape), ptähó-sch (ptahosch; sch slightly hissed).
Flute (with holes for fingering), i̍h-wochka (och guttural).
Fly (v), kikárehdusch (r with the point of the tongue).
Force (v; compel), si̍n-hin-kehde (e distinctly pronounced; in in both cases like i nasal; the whole run together).
Free (he is no slave), waïnihsi̍hnichosch (ch guttural).
Full moon, mi̍hnangkä-okahi̍ (short and run together); it may also be written, mihnang-ga.
Gay-colored, puhsä̍; it is gay-colored, or spotted, puhsä̍hsch.
Go hunting (v; go on a hunt), schánterähusch (an French; e ½; ra short).
God, o̍hmahank-numákschi (an French); literally the lord or chief of the earth.
Good, schihsch (sch often slightly hissed; but not regularly).
Grandchild, tauï̍hangka-sch (hankasch; sch slightly hissed), or tauï̍h-hangkasch.
Grave, there is no such word; burial scaffold, maschóttä; see below, under "inter."
Ground, mánpeterroh (an French; e ½; terroh short and low).
Gums, hiddó-sä (very short and run together).
Gun, wáhta-schirúhpa, or erúhpa (e sometimes pronounced like i); rifle, ehrúhp-achtä̍ (the whole run together).
Hair, pahi̍n (n French; somewhat like a nasal pahi).
Hate (v), woráttehusch (r with the point of the tongue).
Haul (v; fetch), kittáhhusch, or kichkararusch (ich guttural).
Headache, panáhrusch (r with the point of the tongue).
Hear (v), ä-sch (run together; but sch is sometimes prolonged).
Hearty (stout-hearted), kakáhhonsch (on French; sch often a little prolonged).
Heat (v; inflame), manassinko-sch (manassingkosch; sch slightly hissed); i.e., I am warm.
Heaven (sky), cháre-toho-sch (ch guttural; e ½; the whole run together).
Hem (v; clear one's throat), háuikissekusch (the whole run together).
Hole, o̍hoh-pusch (o full; the whole run together).
Hoop (of a barrel), mánna-bihduckä-i̍h-kamenihnde (first e ½).
Hungry, wawarútä-sch; i.e., I am hungry.
Hunter, kaschánteka (an French; e distinctly pronounced).
Ice, chóhde (ch guttural; de distinctly pronounced), or chóhdä.
In (come in), dóbcheta (ch guttural; e ½; ta short).
Inter (v; place on the scaffold), omáhchä-dähhereje (ch guttural; hereje barely audible; je French; e barely pronounced); ohmáhchä, or maschótta, the burial scaffold.
Intoxicate, russidi̍hrusch (r with the point of the tongue).
Kernel (of a fruit or seed), tsúhnta (n French; ta short; uhn somewhat nasal).
Kindle, raptähärri-sch (harrisch very short and indistinct).
Knife, man-hi̍ (man French; often nearly ma with superior o).
Knuckle, assóh-keninde (first e ½; in German; final e distinctly pronounced; the whole run together).
Lament (v; they say "he has pain, he weeps"), náhdä-irratahusch (ch guttural; r with the point of the tongue).
Land, same word as for earth.
Lead, same word as for ball.
Leave (imperative; go out of the way), húh-ketá.
Lick (v), pédeh-sch (first e distinctly pronounced but short).
Life, nán-kesch (an French; kesch moderated; the whole run together).
Long, hánschka (an French; ka short; usually pronounced haschka).
Loose (of clothes), pchi̍hdä (pchi guttural; da short).
Lungs, koppähk (o between a and o).
Marry (v), they say "he has taken a wife," or "she has taken a husband."
Meal (to eat?), warrutó-sch, (warrutosch; sch slightly hissed).
Messenger, kasäddä̍hsch; i.e., I employ him in order to send him.
Mistake (v; lose one's way), chi̍qua-härrisch (ch guttural).
Money, matáschä-schóttä; i.e., the white metal: or okihkikidasusoch; i.e., that which the white men love very much.
Moon, istú-menahke (first e ½; final e distinctly pronounced; the whole run together).
Moonshine, istú-menahke-iddäechosch (e ½; ch guttural; the last two words short and run together).
Mountain, maháhk-chtä̍sch (ch guttural; sch slightly hissed).
Murder (v; same word as for kill), tä̍hrusch.
Music, there is no such word; they say "song."
Naked, ikara-súh-ninakosch (r with the point of the tongue; the whole run together).
Negro, waschi̍psi; i.e., the black man who has everything.
Nest (of birds), tachánde (an French; ch guttural; e distinctly pronounced and short).
Net (fish-net), pó-i̍kuhndä (n French; da very short).
Night, istú-hunsch (istu very short; hun like houn in French).
Nose, páhchu (pah a nasal tone between French ah and an, the same in mahchsi, eagle; chu guttural).
Not (nothing, none), mikóhsch; chosch (ch guttural) is the French pas, or not.
Old woman, rokánka-chihénn (an French; ch guttural).
Oversleep (v; neglect by sleeping), o̍wakinate-kahun-husch (first a distinctly pronounced; n French like oun; the whole short and run together).
Paint (v), uå̍hkapusosch (a somewhat like å, or full).
Palate (roof of the mouth), nuti̍ske-okissángka (e distinctly pronounced).
Partizan (leader of a war party), karókkanakah.
People (lowest people), wáhchikanaschä̍ (ch guttural); this is the most abusive word used by the Mandans.
Pipe (big medicine pipe), i̍h-hinkchóppenih (ch guttural; ihhink run together).
Pipe (tobacco), i̍h-hink-ossúhä (run together); usually ih-hingkä (the whole run together).
Poison, there is no word for it.
Pregnant, ähchichtä̍ (ah rather long; ch guttural; ta short).
Proud, tahuichtä-schi̍hkerisch (u and i separated; ch guttural; ta short; final e ½).
Quick, kattuscho-sch (scho-sch like a subdued schosch).
Rain (n), chä̍h-husch (ch guttural; the whole run together).
Rattle (sysyquoy, gourd rattle), i̍nahdä (nah occasionally like nan in French, nasal).
Ready (completed), wakingkosch; it is not ready, wáuakin-ki̍nichosch (n French; ch guttural).
Rib, dút-huh-dä (da short; the whole run together).
River, passan-hächtä̍ (an French; ch guttural; usually run together, then pronounced passachta, ach guttural).
Rock (cliff), i̍hschanschekeh (an French; first e distinctly pronounced).
Rotten (lazy?), natkachi̍hpo-sch (ch guttural; sch slightly hissed).
Scratch (v), ungkáh-härrisch (harrisch low; the whole run together).
Sea, mönni̍h-kerre, or monni̍h-kärrä (kerre low, even, and without emphasis; e distinctly pronounced but short; r with the point of the tongue).
Shade (shadow), a̍hkunchä (n like French oun; ch guttural).
Shed tears (v; or n, tears?), istámönni-húhrusch (the whole run together).
Shoot (v; with a gun), eruhpákahtä (run together).
Shore (bank), mö̍nnih-wakáchta (kach a strong nasal sound).
Show (v; instruct in a matter), i̍kikuhntäsch.
Sick, ahgä̍nnadusch (also with rusch instead of dusch).
Side (of the body), dóh-i̍schanhä (an French; the whole run together).
Sister (youngest), ptánka (an French); eldest sister, menúkä (e ½).
Sledge (dog-sledge, travail), man-i̍ssischan (an French, but often like a).
Sleepy, hannaruck; I am going to sleep, wahánna-edúck-sanhúsch (an French; the whole short and run together).
Slow, chä̍hrusch (ch guttural; rusch low and short).
Smoke (v; tobacco), manóschhi̍hndusch (short and run together).
Snarl (v; growl), channah-hahosch (ch guttural; the whole run together).
Spark, uarani̍hka (ua almost like wa in the word for fire).
Spoon, mansä̍ (an French); if it is of the horn of the buffalo or bighorn the name of the animal is added.
Spring (the season), bäh-hinundä (n French; the whole run together).
Star, chkäkä (ch begins as a guttural).
Start (v; to start an animal), kachä̍rutosch (ch guttural).
Step-father, called father; likewise step-mother is called mother.
Stifle (v; choke, repress), russi̍ng-ko-sch (russingkosch; sch slightly hissed).
Still, happoähärohn-nkúnihusch (r with the point of the tongue).
Stop (v; stop up), pattarókosch (r with the point of the tongue; o accented).
Storm (they say "a bad day," or "bad weather"), hapä̍h-chikóhsch (ch guttural).
Strong (of drink or other things), páhrusch.
Strong (physical strength), sinhusch (in nasal like i).
Stupid, ochka-sch (ochkasch; och guttural; sch slightly hissed).
Swamp (or lake), manichtä̍; a dirty place, tuntukosch.
Sweet, skunhó-sch (hosch abruptly ended; un like oun in French).
Swim (v), paschún (n French; un like French oun).
Swollen, páh-hosch (run together; sch slightly hissed).
Tear (v; tear or break to pieces), ruchángkosch (ruchangkosch).
Tear out (v), pachkä̍; same as to pluck.
Thick (stout), chtä̍-sch (ch guttural; sch slightly hissed).
Thin, pampi̍h-sch (pampisch; sch slightly hissed; am or an French).
Thunder, chä̍-i-nihä (ch guttural; the whole run together).
Tickle (v), ruksicksikusch (r with the point of the tongue).
Tie (v; fasten), kaskéhje (final e barely audible; j French).
Tobacco (mixed with sakkakomi or bear-berry), mannaschot-kuschä̍.
To-morrow, máhtke (e distinctly pronounced, but short).
Track (of an animal), oni̍hnde (de short; e nearly full value).
Trap (for animals), a̍hchkatachka (ka short; ch guttural).
Turn back (v, return), kiptáhanni-kuhosch (the whole run together).
Void (adj; stale; or cool, moderate), nahnka-wawarut-tenech-osch (first e French and so somewhat nasal; e distinctly pronounced; ch guttural).
War, there is no such word; to fight, ki̍ddack-sahndusch.
War-club (with iron point), mono-pschi̍hdä, or mánna-ókatanhä (an French).
Warmth, same word as for warm.
Warrior (a brave fighter), kirak-san-charakusch (an French; ch guttural; r with the point of the tongue).
Weary, ïua-hatésch (iua separated; h barely audible; e distinctly pronounced; the whole run together).
Weather (fair), happe-schiéhsch (e ½; run together without break); i.e., it is fair weather.
What (or how), taschká-tl (tl lisped as in Mexico).
White-man, waschi̍, or uaschi̍; i.e., he who has everything, or everything good.
Widow, they say "the husband is dead."
Wing (n), ahpcha (ch guttural; final a almost as if with umlaut, short and low).
Woman (wife), mi̍h-hä; this is a woman, mii̍h-husch.
Wound (v), o̍hcha-tu-kä̍rähusch (ch guttural); i.e., he went away wounded.
Yawn (v), ichbedä̍hrusch (ch guttural; sch slightly hissed).
Year, máhna: there is really no word for year; they say "winter,"—"I am so many winters old."
Yes, hon (on French), or hau (pronounced as in German).
Yolk (the yellow in the egg), mándeck-suck-ni̍ïka-kuhschta-ossiidä.
Young animal, koni̍hnka (second n French; ihn somewhat nasal).
Antelope (general term), kokä̍; the buck, kockberockä̍.
Bighorn, ansechtä̍ (an French; e barely audible; ch guttural; ta very short; the whole therefore almost anschta).
Eagle (war-eagle), máhchsi (mah almost like man, French nasal; ch guttural).
Eagle (young bald-headed), chtachtáha (ch and ach guttural).
Elk, o̍mpa, or u̍mpa (om French, um like oum in French).
Gopher (arctomys hoodii, striped prairie squirrel), maschirónika.
Horse, u̍mpa-meni̍ssä (um like oum in French; e ½).
Humming-bird, manasch-chóhpkocháchka (ch guttural; the whole run together).
Otter, pä̍hchtekeh (ch guttural; e ½; keh somewhat prolonged).
Owl (German uhu, strix bubo; western horned owl?), ichki̍hä (ch guttural).
Panther, schuntä̍-háschka; literally the long tail.
Pelican (great, or "scheteck"), nuthkuchtä (uch guttural); i.e., the thick throat.
Rabbit (lepus americanus), máhchtikä (ch guttural; ti short).
Snake, wahchkeruchká (ch guttural; e distinctly pronounced and short).
Swan, mandéh-chóppenih (an French; ch guttural); i.e., the medicine bird.
Swine, waschi̍ta-mató; i.e., the white man's bear.
Turkey (wild), máhnu (a rather full, almost as if with superior o).
Weasel (stoat), máhchpach-pi̍rakä (only slightly separated; ch guttural).
Wolverene (gulo borealis), matóka (ka abruptly ended; run together).
Negundo maple, mi̍hnchka-tah-manaka, (n French, barely audible; last word short and run together).
Willow (salix), háchsä-huhdä (hach with emphasis and nasal; sa and huhda low; ach guttural).
Bracelets of metal, u̍nki-tanhä̍ (n and an French; un like oun).
Hair-ornament (for the front part of head), itáhua-schúngkä (ua separated).
Head-dress (the long feather hood), máhchsi-akub-háschka (German throughout).
Leggings, wapánpi-húnschi (an and n French, like oun).
Necklace of bear's claws, matóunknappi-nihudä (the last two words run together).
Place in a cache (v), mochdaráhkosch (och guttural).
Pouch (for ammunition), mánhä-i̍hdukä, or assóh-kacherúkkä (ch guttural).
Cousin, same words as for brother and sister.
Daughter-in-law, ptaui̍h-hangkasch (au together; ih with emphasis).
Father's brother, same word as for father.
Mother's sister, same word as for mother.
Missouri, Mántahä (an French, rather nasal, like ah).
Chayennes (Chats of the French), Tamáh-ónruschkahpe (on French; e distinctly pronounced; last word low and short; the whole run together).
Grosventres of the prairies, Arrapahó, or Ächichtä-numangkake (ich guttural).
Kayaüas, Káy-ua (the whole run together; u and a separated): the French call them Gens des ptat-côtés [sic].
Pánis, Cháratä-numangkä; i.e., the People of the Wolf, or of the Wolves.

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [256] I am indebted to the untiring patience of Mr. Kipp, who is thoroughly familiar with this language, for this extensive vocabulary which I wrote down with the help of several Mandans. My attempt at a grammar, as I have already said, was interrupted by illness. Mr. Gallatin (ibid., p. 125) includes the Mandans with the Minnitarris; but he had no vocabulary of their language and could, therefore, in no wise form a correct judgment. The signatures to the treaty which he mentions (pp. 125 and 379) were translated into the Minnitarri language because of the lack of a Mandan interpreter. This is shown clearly from the words matsa (man) and lahpeetzee, or lachpitzi (bear), both of which are pure Minnitarri words. I hope by means of the following examples of the Mandan language to refute many of the errors regarding this people which were formerly spread abroad.—Maximilian.
Comment by Ed. For a brief biography of James Kipp, see our volume xxii, p. 345, note 319.

div.head: Notes on the Grammar of the Mandan Language[257]

div.p: Near (German, unweit; French, proche, près de), askásch.
I come from Ruhptare: Ruhptáre ä̍ta wa huh-rusch; i.e., Ruhptare from I come.
I go to Ruhptare: Ruhptáre hiddä wa dä̍hhusch; i.e., Ruhptare to I go.
For "close to" or "hard by," they say also "on the margin of." On the margin of Ruhptare: Ruhptáre i̍wakachta (ach guttural); from i̍wakachta, on the margin of the water, a pond, etc.
There are nearly as many interjections as in our language.
Ä̍h-hä-hä! (run together), an expression of surprise.
Ji̍a (nasal), used in case of exertion which is not wholly successful.
Héi! héi! héi! (German, shrill, pronounced with the tongue), thank you, thank you.
Wáh i sack chárackä! (ch guttural), oh, my God (German, mein Gott)!
Or, does not occur in our form; at least, it is difficult to discover.
A man and a dog, numánk kani manissuérutä.
The one or the other, kotä̍wäcktosch; kitosch signifies that the event is yet to happen.
Kotä̍wa, which is it? in this expression it is difficult to find our word "or."
Gen. The knife of the man whom I have seen: numank uahä̍ssiro óh támanhisch; i.e., the man whom I have seen, this is his knife.
Dat. I will give this to a man and not to a woman: numangkä wáh kuhk tusch mi̍hhä wah wach kuhnichtusch; i.e., to a man I will give it woman I will not give.
Accus. I saw a man do this: numangkä áhska uáhissache uahähsch; i.e., a man this do I have seen.
Abl. The knife comes from the man to whom you have given it: numank dä̍ta mánhi sakuh-rusch-idä̍ta waruschesch.
Dat., to a man, numánk-ä, or numankä̍.
Gen. The head of a man, numank-pa.

Remark. No difference in form is made for sex; and in the case of human beings, appears to be only occasionally indicated by an ending. They say: a man, numánk-máchana; and in exactly the same way, a woman, mi̍hha-máchana; an egg, máh-ni̍hka-máchana. The case where the sexes are indicated is when, for instance, some one addresses a person and tells him he should do something; if it is a man the syllable tá is affixed, if a woman the syllable na.
To be, kitóhsch. This word does not occur frequently.
To be rich: wá kah dä hun; i.e., much wealth.
To be tall is good: háschka kä schihsch; i.e., tall that is good.
I am tall: máh káschkasch; máh, I.
We are tall: núh dä̍ta háschkasch.
You are tall: ni̍h dä̍ta haschkasch.
They are tall: i̍h dä̍ta háschkasch.
I shall do it: waë wasácktosch.
You will do it: wa idá sácktosch.
He will do it: ih wah esácktosch.
We shall do it: nuh dä̍ta esácktosch.
You will do it: nih dä̍ta i̍hda sä̍cktosch.
They will do it: ih dä̍ta ih säcktosch.
Dä̍ta always signifies the plural in this use.
Do not do it: (imperative): káhdä isä̍ckta.
I shall have him (or it): wa káhktosch.
He will have him (or it): ih wa káhktosch; or, in káhktosch (n French; in nasal).
We shall have him (or it): núh káhktosch.
You will have him (or it): wa ra káhktosch.
They will have him (or it): ih onn na káhktosch.
I shall not have him (or it): wa wa kánechosch (ch guttural).

div.head: Singular
div.p: The fish-hook: poïkini̍h (o and i separated).
The branch: o̍hchancha (ch guttural; an French).

div.head: Plural
div.p: The old men: waratóhka-keri̍sch; really keréhsch.
A great forest: mánna-keréhsch; i.e., many trees, from mánna, tree.
Remark. From these instances it is easy to derive the rule that to form the plural of nouns the word keréhsch is affixed. It is occasionally pronounced kerisch, and denotes plurality.
Máhna, the year; the plural is not mána-keréhsch, but manáhna, the years, or better, the winters.

Both arms, i.e., the arms, are called in the plural, a̍hdä-náhta; the legs, dóhke-náhta. This exception is due to the fact that the number of arms on the body is definitely known; they are never more than two, so the plural is "both."

The word keréhsch also signifies in some few cases that objects of only one kind are included, yet always in the plural. Thus, when one enters a lodge where old men or women are assembled, he would say waratóhka-keréhsch, only old men; or rokánka-keréhsch, only or merely old women; waschi̍-keréhsch, merely white men; waschipsi(waschi-psih)-keréhsch, merely negroes, etc.
The word "from," motion towards the speaker, is expressed by tá; as in hutá, come here. The word "to," motion from the speaker, is expressed by the word ä̍ta.
Idä̍ta-keréhsch, the others; in this expression keréhsch is usually omitted, and only idä̍ta used.

The names of these Indians always have a meaning, and often include a whole phrase. All familiar objects and their different states are drawn upon for the names of persons, and these are often very vulgar. I have given some of them above.
Adjectives are placed after the nouns; e.g., meni̍ss-schóttä, horse white, not as in German and English, the white horse.
Mandeck suck-sä (an French), the red bird; i.e., bird the red.
The comparative degree is formed by affixing the word opáchadehsch, or opáchádähsch (ch guttural), i.e., more. The superlative degree is formed by affixing the word mi̍hkasch, i.e., the most.
Good, schihsch: better, schi̍h-opa̍chadehsch: best, schi̍h-mi̍hkasch.
Bad, chi̍cosch: worse, chikä̍-opáchadehsch: worst, chi̍k-ä-mi̍hkasch.
Near, askahá: nearer, aská-opáchadähsch: nearest (next), aská-mihkasch.
Much, hunsch: more, hun (un like French oun)-opáchadähsch: most, hun-mi̍hkasch.
Old, chihósch (ch guttural): older, chihä-opáchadähsch: oldest, chihä-mi̍hkasch.
Sure (certain), does not occur: they say instead, true, tkúschosch; truer, tkschä̍-opa̍chadäsch: truest, tkuscha-mihkasch.
Great (tall), háschka: greater, háschka-opáchadähsch: greatest, ha̍schka-mi̍hkasch.
Wise, schi̍rukosch: wiser, schi̍ruko-pa̍chadähsch: wisest, schi̍ruko-mi̍hkasch.
Remark. Occasionally the comparative and superlative are used together in order to give greater emphasis.
The most beautiful river: pa̍ssanhä(or pássahä)-koschi̍-opachadäh-mi̍hkasch.
The rich man, ko-wakáhdä-hunsch; ko, the.
The poor, ko-áhchkereh-keri̍sch (ch guttural; second e ½).
The beautiful, they say "the good," ko-schi̍hsch.
The colors are expressed in the plural just as in German and English.
The greens (the various greens), wi̍hra-tohä̍-tatá-keréhsch; i.e., wi̍hra-tohä̍, green; tatá, the various.
These answer the question, how many times? or; how often?
A single one, máchana-i̍ncha (in the second word, in almost like i nasal).
Twice, schanáhre-numpóhsch; and so on to and including ten. First, second, third, etc. are expressed in like manner.
Stosch (with the point of the tongue), a single one.
That is much: äth-hunsch (un like French oun).
It is thick: chtä̍hsch; from the word chtä̍, thick.
It is beautiful: schi̍hsch; from schi̍h, beautiful.
In these instances, therefore, sch is added [to form the positive].

div.head: Cardinals
div.p: There are as many expressions for them as in the language of civilized peoples, from one to 1,000,000, etc.
Two, numpä̍ (m French, um like French oum).
Four, tóhpe (e ½); often shortened to tóhp; tóhposch, there are four.
Nine, máchpe (ach guttural; e about ½).
Ten, pitágh (gh guttural); really pi̍rakosch, but it is very much shortened.
One thousand one hundred, isúck-áhga-máchanasch; i.e., eleven hundred.
One hundred thousand, isúck-ikákohi-isuck-mácha-pi̍rakosch; i.e., one thousand ten times one hundred.

div.head: Ordinals
div.p: They continue in like manner, Ko, the, is always prefixed; and hank is always affixed; it is equivalent to German "te," or French ième.

div.head: Fractions
div.p: There is a word for half; the other fractions are expressed by saying "a part."
[No attempt has been made by the translator to rearrange these confused forms.]
I, you, he, we, you, they; she and it are lacking.

row.cell: Gen., of me, man-nan (an French, nasal like ah).
Accus., (or dative; German, uns), us, nuétta.

lg.l: Mi̍h ni̍h rotkä̍, I shall strike you; i.e., I you shall strike.

div.p: You are ashamed of me: man-nan i̍hnkidichihsch (n French; ch guttural); i.e., of me you are ashamed (German, shame yourself).
His eye has served him ill: i̍hta istá i̍h kirúchikosch; i.e., his eye him has served ill; i̍hta istá, his eye.
These notes were interrupted by sickness.

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [257] These were discontinued owing to illness, and are, therefore, incomplete.—Maximilian.

div.head: Mandan Village Dialects
div.p: [The two villages are Mih-tutta-hángkusch and Ruhptáre; the variants are distinguished by prefixing thereto (M) and (R) respectively.—Trans.]
Boat: (M) minnanke (an French; ke short); (R) mánna-kinihnde (de distinct and short).
Bow: (M) woraërúhpa, waraërúhpa, or baraëruhpa; (R) warauïruhpa-gapschihde (e distinctly pronounced).
A child who cries constantly: (M) suck-chámahä-nattach-sinhusch (ach guttural; n French): (R) suckchinick-saráh-sinhusch (e ½; in the second word n is French).
Clothes (article of dress): (M) i̍hmaschuntä (un like French oun); (R) ihmakotä̍.
Cover the fire: (M) uáradä-wakatachta; (R) uaráhdä-wáchkuhárata (the two last words run together).
Covering of a lodge: (M) ti̍hähnachtah (ach guttural; ta long); (R) tihä̍h-karastáh.
Cut meat for drying (v): (M) wahgap-chi̍hda (ach guttural); (R) wahgap-schi̍hdä.
Entrance to a lodge (tambour): (M) berrä-páhchu (r with the point of the tongue; ch guttural); (R) berrä-óschiduhdä.
Fort (of the white men): (M) mannach-kinihnde (ach guttural; e distinctly pronounced); (R) mannách-kini̍hnde (e distinctly pronounced).
Four inner posts of a lodge: (M) tidock-húhdä; (R) mahun-kih-häddä (un like French oun; the last three syllables run together.)
Go and tell this: (M) náhha-ki̍nahta; (R) náhha-kiki̍nihta.
He beats the drum: (M) bäräch-dot-kisch (ach guttural; r with the point of the tongue); (R) bärächt-ki̍h-osch (ach guttural; r with the point of the tongue).
He is here: (M) mánkahusch (an French); (R) a̍hkamehusch (e distinctly pronounced).
He is victorious: (M) wachkaná-hrusch; (R) wachkanná-asch (ach guttural).
He rises (stands up): (M) nán-teh-isch (an French); (R) náh-etosch (e barely audible).
I have found the bones: (M) wahuh-kärrewa-huhsch; (R) húh-kärräwáni-isch (the two last words run together).
I have said it (said so): (M) ä̍h-pisch; (R) wahä̍nni-waä̍h-äs (run together).
I have scraped it (a hide): (M) warrúh-hintuhsch; (R) wapácho-husch (ch guttural).
I sew: (M) i̍wa-tarakosch; (R) kikáh-akosch (a barely audible).
I shall tell him (say to him): (M) wakinnahktusch (run together); (R) waki̍kinihktusch.
I talk with you: (M) waháh-dohrusch; (R) wáhko-haráhrusch.
I think it is so: (M) on-usch-ka-iwa-paschidéhhusch (n French); (R) o̍nschka-ewadehusch.
I throw out the dirt: (M) wapattikosch; (R) wacktóhsch (wack short).
It is sold (the meat): (M) dá-cherä-pusch (ch guttural; r with the point of the tongue); (R) dáhktun-wehdusch (un like French oun).
Lower part of a hill: (M) káh-werisch-kat (e ½);(R) mahä̍h-kar-astá (r with the point of the tongue).
This is medicine: (M) chóppenisch (ch guttural); (R) chóppeni-osch (e short and ½).
One year old buffalo cow: (M) ninkiï-patú (in like i nasal; ii separated); (R) ninkiï-páhtune (e barely audible).
Otter: (M) pä̍hchtekeh, or pä̍chtackä (ach guttural); (R) chóhpäckä (o full).
Pretty: (M) schi̍h-óchadisch (run together); (R) schi̍do-óchorusch (r with the point of the tongue).
Put on your leggings and moccasins: énni-ki̍htata; (R) onni̍h-kihtata.
Scaffold (frame): (M) maschóttä; (R) waschtähn (w like ua; occasionally an e is heard at the end).
Seat yourself: (M) kichkánackta (ich German); (R) nunschiman-hihárata. (n and an French).
Shield: (M) waki̍h; (R) waki̍hdä, or wähkachkopä (ach guttural).
Thank (jemand zum danke streichen): (M) wáhki-ähsch; (R) owáh-kuhunsch (un like French oun).
The water is high (or deep): (M) mönni̍h-pä̍hosch; (R) monnih-kuwuhosch.
They come: (M) hóhrusch (r with the point of the tongue); (R) hóh-usch.
They have shot: (M) erúhpa-ka-tähsch (r with the point of the tongue); (R) erúhpa-ka-tamm-unusch (un like French oun).
They strike one another violently: (M) o̍hki-sa-charakosch (ch guttural; r with the point of the tongue); (R) ki̍hkawo-sin-hosch (in like i nasal).
Thread (n): (M) wäï-wattarakänn; (R) wi̍hkikankähne (n French; e ½).
We have arrived: (M) núhtisch; (R) wä̍h-te-usch (e distinctly pronounced; the whole run together).
You tell the truth: (M) on-usch-kasch; (R) unsch-kusch (un like French oun).
Young cow: (M) ptin-chámahä (in like i nasal; ch guttural); (R) ptin-ihi̍nikä (n as before).

div.head: MINNITARRIS, or Grosventres[258]
div.p: All (the whole, all together), ä̍hsa (sa short).
Answer (v), wih-a-kákiwähs (the whole short and run together).
Arm, a̍hra (r with the point of the tongue).
Ask (v), kiwáschusch (wa very short; chusch low).
Awake (v, intr), mah-kä̍i-sähs. (kai shrill, with the point of the tongue).
Back (adverb), kiï̍ss (ii separated); i.e., he is back.
Back (n, or v; to move with a jerk?), äschitá.
Backward, epéhtïqua (e ½; qua run together and short).
Ball (for playing), maóh-tape (run together; e distinctly pronounced).
Ball-game of the women, ma-úhtape (e distinctly pronounced; the whole run together).
Bear (v; give birth), eïmattúhäs (indistinct and short).
Beautiful, saki̍chtiss (ich with the point of the tongue).
Berdash, biatti̍ (ti short; bi separated from a).
Between, nu-uáh-taru (the whole run together; taru low and without emphasis).
Big with young, same word as for pregnant.
Bile, wáh-aruschi̍de (schi long; de short and low).
Billiard game (Billard-spiel), máh-kache (e ½; the whole short).
Blind, ischtá-läjiss (ji French); i.e., no eyes.
Bone (n), hädú (du very short and explosive; ha almost like German hai).
Box on the ear, ji̍h-tarricki̍ (ii separated; second word short).
Breast (the whole breast), i̍hwaki (ki short, almost like ke).
Brilliant (splendid), hopháh-hischötts (second word low and short).
Brother (youngest), hä̍hderusch (r with the point of the tongue, as always).
Brown, takápiäs (i and a somewhat separated).
Burn (v, reflexive), a̍hotiss (ah and o separated).
Burn (v, tr or intr; destroy by fire), arach-púpiss (run together).
Call (v; call anyone), haä̍hdaha (a and ah separated; daha short).
Calm (n), há-hei-hischess (hei German, together; ha with emphasis; the whole pronounced together).
Canoe, máhn-ti (mahn nasal; n French; ti short).
Carrion (a dead animal), wah-puhä̍s (s barely audible).
Caught (taken pri̍soner), náhchke (nahch long and with emphasis; e ½ and short).
Chill (v; be cold, freeze), mih-áhkapahts (run together).
Coals (glowing), bi̍dda-arra-áracha (the whole run together, short explosive).
Cold (adj), siddi̍h-as (first word with emphasis; as moderated).
Crop (maw), ahpichti̍a (ich German, not guttural; final a ½).
Cure (v), kirai̍schachkais (rai and kais run together; the whole short).
Curry (v; tan), mánpachu (an French; pachu low and short).
Cut down (v), wahk-ksakkes (run together; kes short).
Daughter, same word as for maiden.
Dawn (daybreak), lackscháhwaräs (run together; ras not very short).
Dear (costly), ei̍hwassi-akuss (e short; ih with strong emphasis; the whole run together).
Death's head (totenkopf), dokaráhcha-atú (atu short and explosive).
Die, (v), tä̍es (a and e separated; e ½).
Dirty, awach-sákiss (words pronounced in quick succession).
Divide (v), i̍hwakisshähs (most of the word without emphasis).
Drag (v), rúh-sirruä (ru and a separated; a very short).
Draw (v; draw a load), dúh-särruäs (u separated from as).
Draw (v; draw water), aúschähs (au almost like full o; s indistinct).
Dream (n), same word as for verb.
Dress (clothing), wa-ich-kikschiss (the whole pronounced together), or wikit-schi̍wiss (schiwiss short).
Drink (v), hä̍-ihs (ha loud cry; ihs lower).
Drive (v), nak-hi̍as (hi and as separated; i with strong emphasis).
Ear-ornament, wa-achpóhksche (o very full; e ½).
Early, a̍ntarähts (an French; tarahts low, especially rahts).
Earth, auá (strong emphasis on a; a and u separated, almost like awa).
Egg (of a bird), sakkáh-karáhka; or sakkáh-kanáhka.
Enough, kochk-kats (k half modulated; kats low; the whole run together).
Evening, o̍hksies (o full; sies distinctly pronounced; e ½).
Exchange (v; or mistake), koatóhk-madiäsisch-eschiwáhwarähs (o full; i and a separated; i with emphasis; a ½).
Fade (v; wither), chéhdis (cheh with strong emphasis; dis short and low).
Fall (v; of the leaves), beréhpehahsi̍ss (second e ½).
Fan (of feathers), o̍hhiddi-ächkidda-kóhdi (iddi and idda very short).
Fat (stout), schuwi̍ (wi very short and with strong emphasis).
Festival (corn festival), wah-rui̍kohke (u and i separated; e distinctly pronounced; the whole run together).
Find (v), óhrapiss (o full; piss indistinct and low).
Finger (little), maschákke-káhscha (a only ½, almost like e).
Finger (middle), maschákke-eruhaski (the whole very short and run together).
Finger (third), maschákke-náhschidasche (e ½); i.e., the finger without a name.
Fish (n), buá (a with strong emphasis and rather full, like o).
Fish (v), wóhrak-schi̍ass ( ass like att and indistinct).
Fish (v; catch fish), wóhrak-schi̍es (es together; and distinctly pronounced).
Fist, scháhki-waóhpa-kichkähs (ich German, with the point of the tongue; the whole run together).
Flatter (v), saráhki-páhchus (ki and us lower in tone).
Flesh, erúkschitti (short; schitti short and low).
Force (v; compel), issi̍h-achkehs (the whole short, indistinct, and run together).
Free, arrudi̍tass (di accented; tass sinks in tone).
Freeze (v), maruchán-kapan (an French; kapan indistinct and lower).
Fully, a̍otti (a and o separated; ti low and short).
Go (v), dähts (indistinct and low at the end).
God (lord of life), ehsich-kawáh-hiddisch (hiddisch without accent or emphasis and low; ich German and not guttural).[259]
Good, sakki̍ss (kiss very short; ss barely audible).
Grape-vine, bi̍dda-páheri (pah together; e ½; ri short).
Grass, miká (mi very short; ka strong explosive).
Gray-haired, arrahascheháh-attakits (e ½; its low; the whole short).
Green, maëilö̍üichka (ich with the point of the tongue).
Ground, same word as for earth.
Gums, ihch-schá-arúh-idú (last four syllables run together; idu very short).
Gun, o̍hwa-tsawirúcha (second word short and low); rifle, a̍rruhappissúa (u and a separated).
Hard, sa-su-ki̍ss (sa short; the whole short and run together).
Hate (v), arre-ä̍-wahs (arre short; e ½; the whole pronounced together).
Head, ah-tú (ah nasal; tu very short explosive).
Headache, ah-tú-areä (e ½; last word short and indistinct).
Hearty (stout-hearted), uútahs (uu separated; s somewhat like t).
Heavy, taksi̍äs (as short; i and as separated; i with emphasis).
Help (v), a̍h-pewahais (second word pronounced softly and short; hais German, together; e distinctly pronounced).
Hem (v; clear one's throat), áhpatsekickschiss (strong emphasis on ah; e ½).
Hide (v), a-áchoass (ass low; the whole run together).
Hoarse, erúhschiäs (short and run together; final s distinct).
Hole, máh-arhoppe (e has almost full value).
Hoop (of wood), wirrawáh-apé (ape very short; e ½).
Horn, aaschi̍ (aa separated); or aanschi̍; (a and an French and separated).
Horns, máhroka-ánschi (an French; second a barely audible).
Hot, sawáis (German; the whole short and run together).
Hunger, wah-ahri̍tis; i.e., they are all hungry; mari̍htis, I am hungry.
Hurricane, hóhsi-ichti̍as (ich German and not guttural; i with strong accent; i and a separated).
Incurable, arrukischidä̍hset (dah prolonged with emphasis; arru short).
Jaw, mara-oróhpa (o full; the whole run together).
Knee, wachóh-acha (choh together; the whole pronounced together).
Know (v), ahchkähs (first a ½, almost like a umlaut).
Know (v; be acquainted with), a̍wachkähs (kahs low and moderated).
Lament (v), arra-aki̍wiät; i.e., he weeps from pain.
Land, same word as for earth.
Leap (v; spring), sich-chi̍ss (sich short; chiss likewise).
Left (adverb), i̍rach-ki̍scha (the whole short; scha short).
Lightning, karichkáhs (ich hissed as in German and not guttural).
Long, háski; this word was undoubtedly borrowed from the Mandans.
Loose (of clothes), ichti̍ass (ich German, with the point of the tongue; i with emphasis and separated from ass).
Maiden, bi̍h-akáhsa (final a ½); they also use akáhscha for akáhsa.
Maize, kóhchatä (o full); this word was certainly borrowed from the Mandans.
Medicine-feast (the Okippe of the Mandans), akupéhri (ku very short; ri short and with the point of the tongue).
Medicine-stone, wi̍hdä-katachi̍ (da and chi very short).
Milk (n), ma-áhtsi-biddi̍ (short and run together; biddi very short).
Mirror, ma-ich-ki̍h-ka (ich with the point of the tongue; ka short).
Mistake (v; lose one's way), wachkaráhchisschess (schess low and soft).
Moon, wáhch-kubbedi̍h (the whole short and run togeher; e ½).
Mother, ächká (ach not guttural, but ch hissed).
Music (beat the drum), wi̍rrachárriki (the whole short).
Naked, widdi-bikkikoáejes (e ½; a and e separated; je French; s ½).
Name, náhji (nah with emphasis; ji French, low and short).
Nape (of the neck), machpóh-ottä (together; otta short).
Night, aúk-sïe (auk together, with emphasis; u somewhat like i; si together; e ½, separated and somewhat like a).
Noon, widdiwáh-péirapi (pei together and shrill; the whole short and rapid); i.e., the sun is in the middle.
Nostril, apáre-hopö̍ (e ½; the whole short).
Oldest (the oldest), akouáh-ichti̍äs (o and u separated; ch guttural; ti together; as together).
On the other side, tsóo-ka (ka lowers in tone, short; oo somewhat separated).
On the other side of the hill, awa-itá-sohqua (qua together).
Oversleep (v; neglect by sleeping), hä̍ddauitti̍äs (ti and as separated, ti with emphasis).
Pain (n), hädú-ade-ä̍ss (e ½; strong emphasis on ass; the whole run together).
Palate (roof of the mouth), nóotisch-karuscháscha (oo separated and full; karuschascha short; scha sinks in tone).
Partizan (leader of a war party), akuri̍hdi (di short).
Past (over; go past), eischiss (ei very shrill, with the point of the tongue, with strong emphasis).
Peace, make-itteruchpahk-hatsch (e ½; hatsch low and indistinct, like hahts).
Pinch (v; to carouse?), wirúskapis (pis distinctly pronounced).
Pipe (tobacco-pipe), éikipi (ei very shrill, almost like i and with strong accent; kipi low and short).
Play (v), bidáchatichke (ich German, with the point of the tongue; e ½).
Pregnant, äcdichti̍äs (i with emphasis; i and as separated).
Pretty, sacki̍chtiss (ich with the point of the tongue).
Proud, ichóa-ischi-saki̍ssas (o and a separated; ischi short).
Pulse, dúschi-schi̍äs (i with strong accent; i and as separated).
Push (v; thrust), páki-di̍äs (di and as separated; the whole run together).
Quarrel (v; fight), aúk-schass-hähs (auk with strong emphasis; the whole run together).
Quick, hih-itats (run together; tats low; the whole short).
Rainbow, bi̍ddi-apóka; i.e., the cap of the water.
Rattle (sysyquoy, gourd rattle), éi-poh-chä (ei like ai, together; a loud, shrill fore-tone).
Reconcile (v), make-ikáh-as (e ½; the whole pronounced together).
Red, heischi̍ss (hei together and pronounced very shrilly with the point of the tongue).
Refuse (v; deny), e-ischi̍-arähs (the whole run together); i.e., I will not.
Ring (v), tawóes (o and e separated; es together and ½).
Ripe (of fruit), a̍otiss (ao separated; the whole short and run together).
River, a̍nji-ischti̍äss (first i often silent; j French).
Rock (cliff), bi-hách-pa (hach guttural, yet almost like ha).
Root, äscháhwichkä (wich German, with the point of the tongue).
Run (v), tiriä̍s (s very low and barely audible).
Scaffold (for the dead), mánsachti (man French, long; ti very short).
Scalp (n), biddarú (ru with the point of the tongue, short, and soft).
Sea, bi̍ddi-akichti̍a (biddi very short; first a barely audible; ti and a separated).
Secret (adj), a-achóas (together; as ½ and low).
Shade (shadow), arru-oͣhkse (e ½; o between a and o).
Shiver (v; with cold), wi̍htarichtiss (ich German, with the point of the tongue).
Shooting-star, ichkaró-han-kar-ä̍hs (ich German, with the point of the tongue; an French; the whole run together).
Shore (bank), biddi-däh-tadu; (first and last words very short).
Show (v; instruct in a matter), kikúhs-ki̍ss (short and run together).
Sigh (v), idi̍ahiss (di and a separated; emphasis on i).
Sister, ittawi̍a (first i barely audible; i and a separated, emphasis on i not very strong).
Sit (v), amáhgis (mah very long; gis German guttural).
Sledge, bi̍dda-wa-ádussadua (the whole run together; the last word indistinct and short).
Sleep (v), hi̍ddawiss, or heidabi̍ss (hei shrill, with the point of the tongue).
Smoke (v; tobacco), aúpe-hihs (ua together; e ½).
Snarl (v; growl), eháhte (final e distinctly pronounced; first e short).
Sole (of the foot), ittsi̍-wahú (wahu very short).
Sore-throat, a̍hperu-arreä̍ss (first e distinctly pronounced; last word very short).
Spark (n), bi̍dda-alánka (bidda very short; an French; lan prolonged).
Star, ichká (ich German, with the point of the tongue; ka short).
Steep, nacháppäischass (a and i somewhat separated).
Step-father, same word as for father.
Step-mother, same word as for mother.
Stinginess, márachzats (zats low and indistinct; the whole nasal).
Stomach, bi̍hwaki (bi with stronger accent; i short; waki sinks in tone).
Stone (n), bih-i̍ (i very short and explosive).
Storm (n), maapischi̍a (aa separated; final a short and low).
Strong, iss-hi̍h-äs (run together; strong emphasis on hih; as very short and low).
Sunset, widdi̍-eihwachpiss (ei shrill; pronounced together as in German).
Swamp, biddichti̍a-karä̍hs (i with strong emphasis; ti and a separated).
Sweat-medicine, bih-óh-aku-es (the whole short and run together; oh with strong accent; akues sinks in tone; es short and low).
Swim (v), biddi-di̍hris (biddi very short; the whole run together).
Swollen (swell), póh-ats (ats very soft and low).
Tail (of a quadruped), si̍hta (second i barely audible; ta short; sih long).
Tattooing (n), arukpi̍ (pi with strong emphasis and very short).
Tear (v; tear or break to pieces), duuchä̍hschis (uu separated; schis low).
Teeth, ihch-schá (ihch German, with the point of the tongue; scha short and explosive).
Thumb, scháhkitta, or mascháktá (ta very short).
Tickle (v), wihscheschúkhäs (e ½; has soft and modulated).
Tobacco, aópi (ao somewhat separated; pi short).
Toe, ittsikansa (an French, and prolonged; sa short).
Tongue, däh-eschi (dah with strong emphasis, e ½; and short; eschi short; the whole run together).
Top (summit), awa-áhguka (awa nasal; gu guttural; guka short).
Tree, widá (da short and with emphasis), or bida.
Tremble (v), tadichti̍ss (ich German, with the point of the tongue).
Unmarried, u̍h-arä̍hschis; i.e., he has no wife.
Urine, wä-ä̍h-chiss (chiss guttural, short, and low).
Void (adj; stale; or cool, moderate), wi̍htau-auschirähsches (wih with emphasis; au together).
Wait (v; await), áh-kuch-takahs (ah nasal, with strong emphasis).
War, matauáh-ehá (e ½; aua has each vowel separated); i.e., they are my enemies.
War-club (casse-tête; with the iron point), bi̍dda-i̍hktärrä (tarra very short; bidda likewise), or bi̍dda-aspapsá.
War-club (of stone covered with leather), biï̍-dakútse (bii very short; e ½), or wa-óh-upake (e distinctly pronounced; the whole run together).
War-club (of wood with knots), bi̍dda-pahuachi (the whole short).
Warmth, same word as for warm.
Weather (it is good weather), wáhpe-saki̍ss (e ½, almost like i).
Whirlpool, bi̍ddi-arúhwiddi (widdi very short; likewise biddi).
Whistle (or flute), bi̍dda-kóhotse (o full; ot short; e ½).
Whistle, (v; or pipe), i̍h-akóhsche (a barely audible; e ½).
Widow, there is no corresponding word.
Yawn (v), büidahts (u and i separated; the whole indistinct).
Year, máh-ara (the whole run together; ara very short).
Bracelets of metal, itråuwassa (sa short; the whole short).
Breechcloth, edde̍-ipschake (edde very short; e distinctly pronounced).
Gloves (or mittens), chu-ti̍ (ti short and explosive).
Hair-ornament (flat ornament for the back of the head), arraúhwassa (arra with the point of the tongue; in last word a is only ½).
Necklace of bear's claws, lachpitzi̍-sichpo-ahpöä (run together).
Prairie turnip (pomme blanche, psoralea esculenta), ahi̍.
Bighorn, ansichti̍a (ti and a separated; strong emphasis on ti; first i barely audible).
Buffalo (cow), üichti̍a (ich with the point of the tongue, German; i and a separated).
Deer (common; general term), si̍h-tatacke (e distinctly pronounced).
Deer (stag or buck), si̍h-tatacke-ki̍hrape (e distinctly pronounced); the doe, si̍h-tatackte-mi̍chka (ich German, with the point of the tongue).
Gopher (arctomys hoodii), dáhksassi (sassi even and without accent).
Hedge-hog, apäh-dii (run together; dii slightly separated, almost like di).
Horse, eisóh-waschukka (ei very shrill, with the tongue; second word very short).
Horse (young), éhsu-wassucka-náhnka (some pronounced first word ehsu, others eisoh).
Lynx (wildcat), si̍h-ta-chahe (sih with strong accent; e ½; the whole run together).
Magpie (pica), i̍h-pe (ih with strong emphasis; e ½).
Mink, dacksúa (u with strong emphasis; u and a separated).
Mouse, éhtaho (taho low and short; eh with strong emphasis).
Mule, achichtia (ich German, with the point of the tongue).
Owl (German uhu, strix bubo; western horned owl?), itáhkupä.
Panther, itupáh-ächti̍a (ach with the point of the tongue; i and a separated; i with strong emphasis).
Rat (common, or house rat), ä̍hta-hichti̍a (ti with strong accent, and separated from a).
Rat (wood rat), ai̍hta-hiti̍a (ti and a separated; i with emphasis).
Snake (rattle-snake), arrussidi̍awattú (the whole very short; i and a separated; i with strong accent).
Swan, dúhwisch-scha (the whole run together; duh long and with emphasis; sch very short).
Toad, schánke-káhru (an French; e ½; likewise u).
Turkey (wild), sihs-kichti̍a (run together; ich with the point of the tongue; ti and a separated).
Weasel (stoat), o̍hsisa (oh with special emphasis and force).
Wolf (prairie), bóh-sa (boh long and full; sa very short).
Chayennes, Itáh-ischipáhji (first i very short; the whole short and low).
Crows (the one band), Gi̍hchaitsá; i.e., the fighters for the stomach.
Crows (the other band), Haideróhke; i.e., those who dwell in the middle.
Grosventres of the Prairie, Eirichti̍-aruchpáhga (ei together; tih with emphasis; the whole short).
Mandans (inhabitants of Ruhptare), A̍wa-ichpawati̍ (awa very short; ich with the point of the tongue; pawati short; ti very short).
Muscleshell, Mató-káhsi (o full; si low and short).
Upper Little Missouri, Amáhtikasche (mah nasal; e ½; sche short).
Two, dúupa (uu separated); usually pronounced rúhpa.
Four, tohpá (o full; pa short and explosive).
Five, kechú (e distinctly pronounced; u short and explosive).
Six, akahuá (kah long; wa together and short).
Hundred, pirikchti̍a (ti together and with strong accent; ti and a separated).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [258] Written from the pronunciation of the Indians themselves, especially that of the old chief, Addi̍h-Hi̍ddisch, and with the help of the Mandans who best understood the language. Where no exception is noted, ch always has the guttural sound; r is always spoken with the point of the tongue. Gallatin says that the Minnitarris consist of three tribes, of which two are the Mandans and Annahaways. I have already refuted this statement; besides, the Mandans themselves say that they had nothing in common with the Minnitarris, and that their language was utterly different when they came together; in the case of the Annahaways the statement is equally unfounded, for I could not even find this term, which no one recognized. I have already said that the Minnitarris are a branch of the Crows. These Indians, as well as the Mandans, have not moved their village for many years; they are, moreover, quite safe in them, for Indians do not usually attack fortified places, especially since the two tribes together can at any time put six hundred warriors into the field. Neither did I find among these Indians unusually light complexions nor blue eyes; they do not differ in this respect from the other Indians of the Missouri valley. The legend, likewise, that the Minnitarris are a white race, descended from the Welsh, has just as little foundation, as Gallatin has already shown (ibid., p. 125). Gallatin's words from the Minnitarri language are not correctly written, doubtless through the fault of incompetent interpreters.—Maximilian.
Comment by Ed. See, for the Ahnahaway, our volume xxii, p. 350, note 326.
[259] God is said by some to be called manhopa in this language; but this term was never mentioned to me, and is, therefore, without doubt, incorrect.—Maximilian.

div.head: MUSQUAKE, or Fox[260]
div.p: Buffalo, moskutáck-nallusuá (final a short): i.e., prairie cattle; for they call the domesticated ox, nallusuá.
Devil (evil spirit), matsché-mánito; often shortened to mallato.
Hair, minásse; the red hair-ornament or deer's-tail, kateüikúnn.
Lance (spear), achtauáll (ach guttural; a and u separated).
Otter, kattatawe (w between u umlaut and w; e short).
Sword-lance (lance with a sword blade), táüan (short).
War-club (with the iron point), pakakachkó (ach guttural).
Water, nápch (pch almost like German pich).
White, wapé; wapé-mallato, the white devil; this was the name of the Indian who gave me the words of this vocabulary.
Wood, mattäque (que pronounced separately; e short).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [260] These words were written down from the pronunciation of a Musquake Indian.—Maximilian.

div.head: OJIBUAS, OJIBEUAS, CHIPEWAS, or Algonkins[261]
div.p: Blood, miskui̍ (ui separated; the whole short; emphasis on kui).
Brave (adj), sungedä̍ (su with the point of the tongue); a brave man, mangodas.
Brook, sibins (n French; s soft but audible).
Brother, nitschkoé-esin (esin low, short, and indistinct).
Child (boy), kuiuisän (short and run together; second ui somewhat separated; the whole short; an like French ain).
Child (small girl), squasän (an like French in).
Die (v), nipú (u between o and u).
Enemy, boanack, or poanack; i.e., the Sioux, or Dacota.
Friend (my friend), nsaag-itimih (short and run together); i.e., they love each other.
Healthy, nimino-aïá; i.e., I am well.
Heat, kijachtä̍ (j French; ch barely audible).
Hunger, nuiuissinn (ui separated); i.e., I am hungry.
Meal (or to eat?), uistinnetá (e ½ and short); i.e., let us all eat.
Milky-way (le chemin de St. Jacques), michkanank (ich as in German); i.e., the trail.
Mountain, uattschiu (u and a somewhat separated; i and u likewise).
Small, agaschin (in like i nasal; ga German).

Star, anánk: otschi̍ganank (i.e., the Star of the Pekan, or Fisher), the Wain, or Great Bear; otáhua-moh (les trois rois), "the Three Kings" of the Canadians; makúsch-teguann (run together) the Seven Stars, or the Pleiades; uåh-banank (l'étoile du jour), Venus.
Stingy, sasáhgissi (si short); or shortened to sasáhgiss.
Tomahawk, uagachkuatons-poagann (ach guttural, ons French, but s audible; ann German).
Six, nkótto-uåssoe (soe short; e rather distinctly pronounced).
Seven, nijoåssoe (j French; e rather distinctly pronounced).
Ten, mitassoe (e distinctly pronounced, but short).
Bear (grizzly), ktschi̍-ayáh: when whitish he is called, wåbachquah (ach German and guttural).
Deer (black-tailed deer, cervus macrotis), machkadéh-uanósch: machkadeh, black; uanosch, tail.
Fox (general term), uagóhsch; the name of the color is added.
Lynx (red; felix rufa, le chat sauvage), ä̍h-säbban (sabban short).
Moose (cervus alces), mons (French, but s audible).

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [261] Written from the pronunciation of an Ojibua Indian. The letter l is said to be wanting in this language, and the words given here seem to confirm this view. These Indians received the name Sauteurs from the French, because they lived at the falls (sauts) of St. Anthony. They are commonly called Chipeways (Tschipewäs); but pronounce this name, themselves, Ojibua.—Maximilian.
Comment by Ed. The name "Saulteurs" was derived from the residence of these Indians at Sault Ste. Marie.

div.head: OMAHA[262]
div.p: Alone, snog-djé (j French; g almost like German ch).
Awake (v, intr), wåtómbe-najeh (j French; e distinctly pronounced).
Awake (v, tr), ih-ki-räh (the whole even); same word as in the Oto language.
Backward (back), charah (ch guttural); charah-monni, go back, return.
Beautiful, oh-campé (campe French; the whole pronounced together).
Bitter, ski-da-jä (j French); i.e., not sweet.
Blind (adj), ischtá-uäraje (je French; final e distinct).
Burn (v; consume by burning), nåh-chu-dä̍ (ch guttural).
Cave, mon-schont-djé (on French, likewise j; e audible).
Clear (bright), kéhra (ra with the point of the tongue).
Convenient (comfortable), same word as for good.
Deaf, nåh-chiddä-ning-gä (ch guttural; the whole run together).
Dirty (v; or adj), må-cherihcherih (ch guttural; e very short; the whole short).
Dwelling place (hunting stand), goss-sin (in like i nasal).
Face (sight), indjäh (i barely audible; j French).
Fall (v) gochhiára (ch guttural; the whole short).
Finger, nombä̍; same word as for hand.
Flee (v; escape), o̍nhä (on French, and nasal).
Forget (v), gih-sirajäh (j French; the whole run together).
Good, udá; the best, eh-jna-udá (j French).
Green, tuch-tsche (e short); i.e., literally, very blue.
Grow (v), granräh-tigräh (an French; gr with the point of the tongue).
Gun, uahutan (ua like wa; an French).
Hear (v), nåhk-on (on French; the whole run together).
Hide (v), na-che-ran (ch guttural; an French; e short).
Horse (a young horse), schantón-schi̍nga (an and on French; first word with emphasis; second without).
Know (v; be acquainted with), ih-pahán (pa short; an French).
Leaf, jån-hich-pä (jan French; final e distinct).
Lie (v; deceive), i-uh-sisch-tan (an French; the whole run together).
Maiden, mi̍h-jinga (mih with emphasis; ji French; jinga without emphasis).
Mirror, ni̍o-kigrásse (a audible; i and o separated).
Moon, mih-om-ba (mih with emphasis; the whole run together).
Nail (on hand, foot, hoof, claw), schagä̍.
Oldest, jini̍ (j French); my oldest brother, vijini̍.
Peace, manchon-úda (an and on French); i.e., not war.
Pray (v), wåkonda-berihs-tubä̍ (e short; otherwise German throughout).
Powder (gun-powder), måh-chudä̍ (ch guttural; the whole run together).
Shoot (v; with a gun), wåhutonwåkiddäh (on French).
Sit (v), gerin (e short; r with the point of the tongue; in like i nasal).
Son, ji-ingä̍ (j French; the whole run together).
Stone, ih-in (n French; in like i nasal).
Swim (v), ni̍huan (an French); same word as in the Oto language.
Tear (v; tear, or break to pieces), ih-bråh-sä (ah French; sa short).
Tomahawk, mǻse-päji̍inga (se short; j French; last word rapidly pronounced).
Tongue, rä̍hse (e distinctly pronounced); téh-rähs, buffalo tongue.
Unhealthy (sickly), wåh-kägaschtån (the whole even and run together).
Unripe, nihd-aije (ai together; j French; e low but distinct).
Wax, kegranchä-uägrä (an French; ch guttural; g with the point of the tongue).
Whirlpool, nih-berih-berin (short and run together; e short; in like i nasal).
Eight, péh-rǻbene (first e short; second e audible).
Panther, igronga-sindä̍-snaddäh; sindä-snaddäh, with long tail.

div.head: FOOTNOTES:
div.p: [262] Written from the pronunciation of Major Dougherty, who understood this language perfectly. The Omáhas belong to the Dacóta linguistic group, and form with the Osages, Konzas, Ayowäs (Joways), Missouris, Otos, and Puncas, Mr. Gallatin's southern Sioux. Among the nations named there are several different dialects, of which the Osages and Konzas speak one; the Otos, Ayowäs, and Missouris another; and the Omahas and Puncas a third. On these peoples, see Gallatin (ibid., pp. 126-28). There it is noted that a vocabulary of the Ayowäs (Jówäs) is lacking; a gap which I can claim to have filled, since I was assured by Major Dougherty that the Ayowäs speak the Oto language, whose words are given below.—Maximilian.

div.head: OTO[263]
div.p: All (all together), brogä̍; the whole mass (or multitude), akiwoasan (woa like voi in French; an French).

list.item: I myself alone, mij-nå (j French here and below).

div.p: American (an), Måhi-hónn-ie (ie short; e audible); i.e., Long Knife.
Ball (bullet), måh-seh-måh; same word as for lead.
Bird, wåe-ing-ä (e barely audible; the whole together).
Bitter, sehko-schkunä̍; i.e., not sweet, they do not have a direct expression.
Blind, ich-tåch-hidje (j French; final e short).
Breath, hi̍; same word as for mouth and tooth.
Brown, chudje (ch guttural; e distinctly pronounced); i.e., dark, smoky, they have no word for brown.
Buy (v), wå-ru-mäh; same word means to trade.
Carrion (a dead animal), uå-hu-mä̍ (ua short and together).
Caught (v; captured), ua-ni-hih (u and a separated).
Cave, i̍ro-chrogä̍; i.e., a hollow rock.
Chew (v), same word as for meal, or to eat.
Child, tchitching-ä (ch like tgi, with the point of the tongue).
Choke (v; press to death, smother), o-nong-ä̍.
Clear (water), ni-bréjé (French); they give this name to the Mississippi.
Comb (n), härusäh, i.e., louse-catcher; from hä, louse, and rusäh, catch.
Community (company, many men), manksché-gerohan (an French; ge German).
Convenient (comfortable), pi̍; same word as for good.
Cowardly, same word as for lazy, or rotten.
Crow (way of dressing hair), nantó (an French).
Cut into (v; incise, carve), grontsché (on French).
Day, han-uä (an French, the whole short and run together).
Deaf, nå-cho-dje-ning-e (j French; ch guttural; e short).
Decoy (v; decoy an animal), tah-sching-ä-on (sching and a pronounced together; on French).
Dirty, måh-chrih (ch with the point of the tongue).
Dive(v), ni̍h-rotata. [MS. note in Library of Congress copy by J. O. Dorsey, says that this is not a verb but ni, water, and rótata, under.—Trans.]
Double, nouä̍; same word as for two.
Drag (v; drag a load), påhi̍-on-reh (on French).
Dust, månschuh-schudje (an French; likewise j; e short).
Dwelling place (hunting stand), irappä (final a between e and a umlaut).
Ear-ornament, uåhnon-pin (non French; pin nasal, like pi).
Early, heruh-tach-tsché (ach guttural); early in the day.
Even (equal, flat), bra-ské, or bras-ké; same word as for broad, or great.
Evening, pi̍-kuiä̍, or pi̍kuiä̍; from pi, sun, and kuiä̍, low.
Everywhere, mayon-brughä (on French); i.e., over the whole land.
Eye, ichtá (ich German and not guttural; nearly the same as with the Dacota, Omahas, Osages, and Puncas).
Feast, same as meal, or eat; they say, give to eat; also gi-ko.
Fire, pedjé (first e distinctly pronounced; j French).
Fish (v; catch fish), same word as for fish-hook.
Frenchman, Måsongkä-okannä (a umlaut, also pronounced like e).
Gun, jútschä (tscha short); rifle, jútschä-ki̍h-berúh-berúh (the whole short, and run together).
Gut (v; gut an animal), nicha-gi-na-sché (ch guttural).
Half, oskisserä (e short); så-ning-ä̍, the second part.
Heart, mon-tchä (on French; ch with the point of the tongue).
Heat (v; inflame), tåcherang (ch guttural); i.e., warm; they also say monschtiö (on French).
Hollow (adj), chro-gä̍ (ch with the point of the tongue).
Iron, mǻ-sä (first syllable longer; first a almost like an French).
Lance (spear; sword-lance), uåh-yaueh (letters in yaueh are separated).
Leader (chief), uong-gé-gi-hi (first syllable almost like wong; g guttural).
Light (v; illuminate), hån-ue-on-re (an and on French; ue nasal, likewise han).
Light (v; kindle), ohan-ue (an French; u and e separated).
Like (v; be fond of), ooch-thá (ch guttural).
Man, uong-gä, or uong-äh; same word as for human being.
Money, må-ses-kå (all syllables even); i.e., white metal.
